code to check which are continuous and which are ordinal
```{r}

# Function to classify variables
classify_variable <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    nunique <- length(unique(x[!is.na(x)]))
    
    if (nunique <= 10 && all(x %% 1 == 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      return("ordinal")
    } else {
      return("continuous")
    }
  } else {
    return("other")
  }
}

variable_types <- sapply(env_vars, classify_variable)

classification_result <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(variable_types),
  Type = variable_types
)

print(classification_result)

continuous_vars <- names(variable_types[variable_types == "continuous"])
ordinal_vars <- names(variable_types[variable_types == "ordinal"])
other_vars <- names(variable_types[variable_types == "other"])

cat("\nContinuous variables:\n", paste(continuous_vars, collapse = ", "))
cat("\n\nOrdinal variables:\n", paste(ordinal_vars, collapse = ", "))
cat("\n\nOther variables:\n", paste(other_vars, collapse = ", "))


```

:) RUNNING PCA ON A CLEANED VERSION OF DATASET 

Did this on cleaned as PCA does not work when there are NA parts in the dataset.

```{r running pca on cleaned}
env_vars_numeric <- env_vars_cont[, sapply(env_vars_cont, is.numeric)]

variances <- apply(env_vars_numeric, 2, function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return(NA)  
  } else {
    return(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  }
})

valid_cols <- !is.na(variances) & (variances != 0)

env_vars_filtered <- env_vars_numeric[, valid_cols]

anyNA(env_vars_filtered)
any(is.infinite(as.matrix(env_vars_filtered)))

#remove rows with any NA value
env_vars_clean <- env_vars_filtered[complete.cases(env_vars_filtered), ]
pca_result_sc = prcomp(env_vars_clean, scale=TRUE)

summary(pca_result_sc)
```

Plotting the result of principal components vs stdeviations
```{r}

plot(pca_result_sc)
```

:) decide on how many components to keep using cumulative PVE

here plot stops changing alot after 4th component
```{r}
prop_var_expl_sc = summary(pca_result_sc)$importance[2,]
cumul_prop_var_expl_sc = summary(pca_result_sc)$importance[3,]

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(prop_var_expl_sc, type="b", xlab="Component number (sc.)",
ylab="Proportion variance explained", ylim=c(0,1) )
plot(cumul_prop_var_expl_sc, type="b", xlab="Number of components (sc.)",
ylab="Cumulative prop. var. expl.", ylim=c(0,1) )
```
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________

_____________________________________________________________________________________________________
:) calculating second order difference ratio to help detect elbow point
```{r}
cumul_prop_var_expl <- cumul_prop_var_expl_sc
nElem=length(cumul_prop_var_expl_sc)
ratios=(cumul_prop_var_expl[2:(nElem-1)]-cumul_prop_var_expl[1:(nElem-2)])/
(cumul_prop_var_expl[3:nElem]-cumul_prop_var_expl[2:(nElem-1)])
ratios
```
max operator tells where explained variance is sharpest.

according to this the first 34 components must be retained
```{r}
nComponents_selected = which.max( ratios ) + 1
nComponents_selected
```

:) biplotting original variables against 2 PCs

The biplot below shows 2 components :
1. arrows (results from pca_result$rotation)
2. points (results of pca_result)

Rotation transforms original variables into principal components.
Rotation is needed in order to tell how much each original variable loads onto each PC.
And arrow lenghts are determined by this rotation.

Each arrow corresponds to the original variable in our dataset.
The direction and length of an arrow indicate how strongly that variable contributes to the PCs. 

Longer arrows means that the variable is well represented by the first 2 PCs and has a strong influence.Short arrows mean that the variable is weakly represented and less imp in these 2 components. 

The angle between the arrows represents the correlation between variabels. 
Small angles means that the variables are +vely correlated.
angles around 90 means that the variables are uncorrelated.
angles close to 180 mean that they are -vely correlated.

```{r}
pca_result <- prcomp(env_vars_clean, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE) 

graphics.off()

dev.new(width=100, height=100, unit="in", noRStudioGD=TRUE)

fviz_pca_biplot(pca_result, repel = TRUE, arrowsize=1.5,col.var="#A2E6FF",xlim=c(-5,5),ylim=c(-5,5),
       cex=1.2,           
       expand=3)

summary(pca_result)
```

:) rotate all 9 components using oblimin

```{r}
install.packages("psych")

unrot9 = round(pca_result_sc$rotation[,1:4], 3)

```
h2 represents communality, u2 represents uniqueness and com represents complexity.
lets take a row: ndyprmpm10  -0.24	0.77	0.21	-0.08	0.8481608	0.15183922	1.366687

strong loading on MR2, low loadings on other factors. so its not complex
the h2 is 0.8481608, the u2 is 0.15183922 and com is 1.366687.
85% of the variance of ndyprmpm10 is explained by the 4 factors.
15% is unexplained.
complexity is 1.4 mostly loads on 1 factor so has very clean strucutre.

Our loadings matrix shows that many varibale have weak or scattered contributions across components.

Many variables e.g ndyprmpm10, ndyprmpm2_5, ndyprmno2, ndyprmo3, ndyprm, ndyprypm10, ndyprypm2_5, ndypryno2, ndypryo3, ndypry, 
tmpdca, tmpdcmx, tmpdcmn, tmpdcaw, tmpdcam, tmpdcay, tmpdcacm, tmpdcamb, tmp95pacmb, tmpanocm, pacctaw, pacctam, pacctay, pacctcm, pacctmb, paccdcm, iwg10mxam, iwg10mxa3m, iwg10mxay, iwg10mxamb load heavily on one PC. This means that these variables are captured by a single underlying latent factor. These variables should be retained, not removed.

You should consider removing those varibales that have low commonalities, high complexity and cross loadings.

cross loadings (those that load moderately on multiple PCs) --> ndypryo3, ndyprm, tmpdcay, tmpdca3m, iwg10mx, iwg10mxam, iwg10mxay, iwg10mxamb. 

low communalities (h2) --> only a small portion of a variable is explained by these 
common (underlying) factors. here it is ndyprmo3, tmpdca3m, tmpanod, tmpanocm, paccta, pacctaw, iwg10mx, iwg10mxaw, iwg10mxay.

high complexities (com) -->ndypryo3, ndyprmpm2_5, ndyprm, tmpdca3m, paccta3m, iwg10mx, iwg10mxaw, iwg10mxay, iwg10mxamb. 

thus we need to remove:ndyprmpm2_5, ndyprm, paccta3m,iwg10mxaw, ndyprmo3, tmpdca3m, tmpanod, tmpanocm, paccta, pacctaw, iwg10mx, ndypryo3, tmpdcay, iwg10mxam, iwg10mxay, iwg10mxamb

:) FINAL CONCLUSION for CONTINUOUS portion of dataset

Here the analysis is telling us that we still have low contributing variables of "tmpdcmx", "tmpdcamb", "tmpdcaw", "tmpdca", "tmp95pacmb", "tmpdcam", "tmpdcmn" that we can remove. I know that I said earlier that some these load heavily on only one PC and are useful for our analysis but from the scree plot and overall contribution patterns it is clear that the impact on total dataset variance is limited.

Thus all variables to remove from the continuous portion of the dataset becomes:ndyprmpm2_5, ndyprm, paccta3m,iwg10mxaw, ndyprmo3, tmpdca3m, tmpanod, tmpanocm, paccta, pacctaw, iwg10mx, ndypryo3, tmpdcay, iwg10mxam, iwg10mxay, iwg10mxamb

```{r}

```

```{r}
ordinal_var_names <- c(
  "aqiwdpm10", "aqiwdpm2_5", "aqiwdso2", "aqiwdno2", "aqiwdo3", "aqiwd",
  "aqiw2dpm10", "aqiw2dpm2_5", "aqiw2dso2", "aqiw2dno2", "aqiw2do3", "aqiw2d",
  "ndyprwpm10", "ndyprwpm2_5", "ndyprwso2", "ndyprwno2", "ndyprwo3", "ndyprw",
  "ndyprmso2", "ndypryso2"
)

env_ordinal <- env_vars[, colnames(env_vars) %in% ordinal_var_names]
env_ordinal[] <- lapply(env_ordinal, function(x) {
  if (!is.ordered(x)) ordered(x) else x
})

#filter out variables with only one unique value
valid_cols <- sapply(env_ordinal, function(x) length(unique(na.omit(x))) > 1)
env_ordinal_filtered <- env_ordinal[, valid_cols]

#filter out variables with near zero variance
nzv <- sapply(env_ordinal_filtered, function(x) sd(as.numeric(x), na.rm = TRUE) < 1e-6)
env_ordinal_filtered <- env_ordinal_filtered[, !nzv]

env_ordinal_clean <- env_ordinal_filtered[complete.cases(env_ordinal_filtered), ]

hetcor_result <- hetcor(env_ordinal_clean)
poly_corr <- hetcor_result$correlations

bad_cells <- which(!is.finite(poly_corr), arr.ind = TRUE)
bad_vars <- colnames(poly_corr)[unique(c(bad_cells[,1], bad_cells[,2]))]
env_ordinal_clean_fixed <- env_ordinal_clean[, !colnames(env_ordinal_clean) %in% bad_vars]

hetcor_result <- hetcor(env_ordinal_clean_fixed)
poly_corr <- hetcor_result$correlations

stopifnot(all(is.finite(poly_corr)))


fa.parallel(poly_corr, n.obs = nrow(env_ordinal_clean), fa = "pc", fm = "pa")

ordinal_pca <- principal(poly_corr, nfactors = 2, rotate = "none")

print(ordinal_pca)

```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# Convert loadings to a data frame
loadings_df <- as.data.frame(ordinal_pca$loadings[, 1:2])
loadings_df$varname <- rownames(loadings_df)

ggplot(loadings_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = varname)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "#A2E6FF") +
```

plot pca of original data2 with these variables removed

```{r}
data2 <- data

# Step 1: Define variables to remove (e.g., redundant or irrelevant)
vars_to_remove <- c(
  "ndyprmpm2_5", "ndyprm", "paccta3m", "iwg10mxaw", "ndyprmo3", 
  "tmpdca3m", "tmpanod", "tmpanocm", "paccta", "pacctaw", 
  "iwg10mx", "ndypryo3", "tmpdcay", "iwg10mxam", "iwg10mxay", "iwg10mxamb"
)

# Step 2: Remove unwanted variables
data2_clean <- data2[, !names(data2) %in% vars_to_remove]

# Step 3: Select only numeric columns
numeric_columns <- sapply(data2_clean, is.numeric)
data2_numeric <- data2_clean[, numeric_columns]

# Step 4: Remove rows with missing values
data2_numeric_complete <- na.omit(data2_numeric)

# Step 5: Remove columns with zero variance
variances <- sapply(data2_numeric_complete, var)
nonzero_columns <- variances != 0
data2_numeric_filtered <- data2_numeric_complete[, nonzero_columns]

# Step 6: Run PCA on cleaned numeric data
pca_result <- prcomp(data2_numeric_filtered, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

# Step 7: Plot the PCA biplot
fviz_pca_biplot(
  pca_result,
  repel = TRUE,              # Avoid overlapping text
  arrowsize = 1.5,           # Size of variable vectors
  col.var = "#FF7F7F",       # Soft red for variable arrows
  cex = 1.2,                 # Scaling for text
  xlim = c(-5, 5),           # X-axis limits
  ylim = c(-5, 5),           # Y-axis limits
  geom.ind = "none",         # Do not plot individual observations
  title = "PCA Biplot of Data (After Variable Removal)"
)
```

```{r}
library(psych)
vss_result <- VSS(data2_numeric_complete, rotate = "none", fm = "pc")
plot(vss_result)
```

LOADINGS with all PCs found on the entire dataset 


Even though I have dropped weak or problematic variables after running a PCA and selected an optimal number of components on the original dataset it is better to return to the full loading matrix. It ensures:

- I preserve a complete mapping from original variables to selected components.
- I  can later project any future or external data in the same feature space without re-training or re-rotating.
- I  keep the same coordinate system (orthogonal PC axes) established by the initial PCA.

```{r}
loadings_all_optimal <- pca_result_sc$rotation[, 1:nComponents_selected]
round(loadings_all_optimal, 3)
```
